en: Then, in order to resolve these four questions beginning with "What are those [tantras] of the Yoginītantra?", he says: "Now," and so forth.
"Now I shall declare another certainty regarding the Yoga-tantra;
the authoritative measure of the Yoginītantra is also being told—listen, O Guhyaka! (22.1)
The Yoga Tantra is indeed measured at sixty million,
while the Yoginī Tantra is said to number sixteen million.
The Mahāyāna has its own distinct collection of sūtras, said to number eighty koṭis; and the Pāramitā-naya likewise consists of fifty lakṣakoṭis.
"Of the Mahāyāna" means from the Mahāyāna. "Separately" refers to the Śrāvakayāna.
These all that have been spoken by the Lords of Munis, possessing the form of the three bodies, constitute the teaching of the Sugata. 22.4

"All these that have been mentioned" means all these aforementioned ones. "By the lords of sages" means by the *munīndras*. "Possessing the form of the three bodies" means by those having the forms of the three bodies. "The teaching of the Sugata" is the conclusion; the meaning is that the teaching of the Sugata is of such a nature.
To the question, "With reference to whom was what taught?", he says: "The Vinaya," and so forth.
All [the teachings], beginning with the *Vinayapiṭaka*, as well as the self-teaching among the *Śrāvakas*—
The teaching for the bodhisattva is the great commentary on various sūtras.

The secret of the *Yogayoginītantra* is the domain of the Buddhas. The locative case in "among the *śrāvakas*" (*śrāvakeṣu*) refers to persons belonging to the *Śrāvakayāna*, and it is used in the sense of a "locus" (*nimitta-saptamī*). "Instruction for oneself" (*ātmadeśanā*) means instruction for the purpose of self-taming, tranquility, and so forth. "Great speech" (*mahābhāṣam*) refers to those sūtras that serve as commentaries on other sūtras. "Of the Bodhisattva" (*bodhisattvasya*) means for the sake of one who possesses the Bodhisattva lineage. In the phrase "of the *Yogayoginītantra*," the genitive case is used in the sense of the first case (i.e., denoting the subject). Regarding "the domain of the Buddhas" (*buddhagocaram*), the ellipsis is "with respect to sentient beings"; it is so called because the Buddha alone is its domain.
By this it is stated that the teaching of the method of mantra is for the sake of one of great wisdom. As it is said in the *Cittaviśuddhi*:
"The greatness of the Mahāyāna is the domain of the Great Being.
(*Cittaviśuddhiprakaraṇa* 86ab, 84cd)
Thus it is said. Furthermore, elsewhere:
"Even though the goal is the same, the system of Mantra is distinguished by its lack of confusion, its many methods, its lack of difficulty, and its being intended for those of great wisdom."
Thus, the hallmark verse of the *Nayatrayapradīpa*:
"For sentient beings of meager merit, the teaching [is given] in the form of a deity. (22.6)
The visualization of the Dharmakāya, Sambhogakāya, Nirmāṇakāya, and Mahāsukhakāya—the yoga whose nature is wisdom and means—swiftly brings about Buddhahood. (22.7)

To the question, "From where does this variety of teachings arise? he says: "Those of meager merit. The sense is that beings of meager merit attain discipline (*vinaya*) gradually. Alternatively, for the sake of beings of meager merit, there is the teaching in the Mantra system consisting merely of the form of the deity. For, by relying on the form of the deity, one cultivates the body of phenomena (*dharmakāya*) and so forth; and by relying on that, one cultivates the union of wisdom and means, whose nature is emptiness and compassion.

In the Mantra system, these two types of paths—consisting of the stages of generation (*utpattikrama*) and completion (*utpannakrama*), and characterized as cause and fruit—have been demonstrated. And this [path] brings about Buddhahood swiftly, because one possessing diligence attains Buddhahood in this very life.
